title: How to diagnose thread deadlock — thread dump shows threads in BLOCKED state waiting for each other's locks — fix by consistent lock ordering, shorter critical sections, or using `tryLock` with timeout?
shortTitle: How do you diagnose a thread deadlock?

s1_definition.profdef: A deadlock occurs when two or more threads each hold a lock the other needs and neither will ever release, so all of them wait forever. You diagnose it from a thread dump, where the deadlocked threads appear in the BLOCKED state, each "waiting to lock" a monitor that another thread "holds." Modern JVMs even print an explicit "Found one Java-level deadlock" section. You fix it with consistent global lock ordering, shorter critical sections, or lock acquisition with a timeout using `tryLock`.
s1_definition.analogy: Picture two tellers at National Bank of India processing a transfer between Rajesh and Priya. Teller A locks Rajesh's ledger and then reaches for Priya's ledger, while at the same moment Teller B locks Priya's ledger and reaches for Rajesh's. Each is holding the exact book the other needs, and each refuses to let go until they get the second book. They will both wait forever, and both transfers freeze. That is a deadlock. The fix is a branch rule that everyone always picks up the lower account number's ledger first, so this standoff can never happen.
s1_definition.oneliner: A deadlock is threads holding each other's locks forever; find it in a thread dump's BLOCKED threads and fix it with consistent lock ordering or tryLock with a timeout.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A deadlock occurs when two or more threads each hold a lock the other needs and neither will ever release, so all of them wait forever. You diagnose it from a thread dump, where the deadlocked threads appear in the BLOCKED state, each "waiting to lock" a monitor that another thread "holds." Modern JVMs even print an explicit "Found one Java-level deadlock" section. You fix it with consistent global lock ordering, shorter critical sections, or lock acquisition with a timeout using `tryLock`.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Picture two tellers at National Bank of India processing a transfer between Rajesh and Priya. Teller A locks Rajesh's ledger and then reaches for Priya's ledger, while at the same moment Teller B locks Priya's ledger and reaches for Rajesh's. Each is holding the exact book the other needs, and each refuses to let go until they get the second book. They will both wait forever, and both transfers freeze. That is a deadlock. The fix is a branch rule that everyone always picks up the lower account number's ledger first, so this standoff can never happen.

**One line to remember:** A deadlock is threads holding each other's locks forever; find it in a thread dump's BLOCKED threads and fix it with consistent lock ordering or tryLock with a timeout.

sections.s2_technical:
A deadlock needs four conditions to hold at once: mutual exclusion (locks are exclusive), hold-and-wait (a thread holds one lock while waiting for another), no preemption (locks cannot be forcibly taken away), and circular wait (a cycle of threads each waiting on the next). Break any one condition and deadlock becomes impossible. The most practical condition to break is circular wait, which you eliminate by always acquiring locks in a consistent global order.

To diagnose a deadlock, you take a thread dump with `jstack <pid>` or by sending the JVM a quit signal. In the dump, deadlocked threads are in the BLOCKED state. Each one shows a line like "waiting to lock <0x...>" naming the monitor it wants, and "locked <0x...>" naming the monitor it already holds. By following these, you see thread A holds monitor 1 and wants monitor 2, while thread B holds monitor 2 and wants monitor 1 — a cycle. The HotSpot JVM detects this and prints a clear "Found one Java-level deadlock" block that names both threads and the locks, so you rarely have to trace it by hand.

The fixes follow from breaking circular wait. First, consistent lock ordering: define a stable order for locks, for example by account number or object identity hash, and always acquire them in that order so a cycle cannot form. Second, shorter critical sections: hold each lock for as little code as possible, and never call out to unknown code while holding a lock, which reduces the window for contention and deadlock. Third, timed locking with `tryLock`: instead of blocking forever on `synchronized`, use a `ReentrantLock` and call `lock.tryLock(timeout)`, so if a thread cannot get the second lock in time, it backs off, releases what it holds, and retries, which breaks the hold-and-wait condition.

A senior nuance: programmatically you can detect deadlocks at runtime with `ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads()`, which is great for a health check that logs and alerts if any deadlock ever forms. Also distinguish deadlock (threads BLOCKED forever, no progress) from livelock (threads active but making no progress) and from simple lock contention (threads wait but eventually proceed). Only true deadlock never resolves on its own.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's transfer service deadlocked when two transfers ran at the same time in opposite directions: one from Rajesh to Priya and one from Priya to Rajesh. Each thread locked the source account first, then blocked trying to lock the destination. This is exactly the circular-wait deadlock.

Problem 2 — The service hung with no errors and no CPU usage; nothing progressed. This is exactly the BLOCKED-forever signature that a thread dump reveals, distinct from a busy infinite loop.

Problem 3 — We need both to detect it automatically and to prevent it. This is exactly where `ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads()` detects it and consistent lock ordering (or tryLock) prevents it.

Our mini-project builds a `DeadlockDemo` with a naive transfer that locks accounts in call order (causing deadlock), a `DeadlockDetector` that uses `ThreadMXBean` to find and log any deadlock, and a `SafeTransferService` that fixes it by always locking the lower account id first. The reader sees the deadlock form, gets it detected, then sees the ordered version run cleanly.
sections.s4a_structure:
```
jvm-deadlock-demo/
├── pom.xml
└── src/
    └── main/
        └── java/com/bank/jvm/
            ├── DeadlockDemo.java          (main runnable demo)
            ├── Account.java               (lockable account)
            ├── NaiveTransferService.java  (deadlocks: locks in call order)
            ├── SafeTransferService.java   (ordered locking, no deadlock)
            └── DeadlockDetector.java      (ThreadMXBean deadlock detection)
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile
javac -d target/classes src/main/java/com/bank/jvm/*.java

# Run: watch the naive transfers deadlock, get detected, then safe transfers succeed
java -cp target/classes com.bank.jvm.DeadlockDemo

# The REAL production procedure: take a thread dump of the hung process
jstack <pid>                    # look for "Found one Java-level deadlock"
#   BLOCKED threads show: "waiting to lock <0x..>" and "- locked <0x..>"
# Or send a quit signal to print a dump to the app's stdout:
kill -3 <pid>
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: two accounts, Rajesh SAV2001 and Priya CUR3001, with two simultaneous opposite transfers.

Step 1 — Thread txf-R-to-P calls the naive transfer and locks Rajesh (the source). It then sleeps briefly, simulating work inside the critical section.

Step 2 — At the same time, thread txf-P-to-R locks Priya (its source). Now txf-R-to-P holds Rajesh and wants Priya; txf-P-to-R holds Priya and wants Rajesh. A cycle has formed.

Step 3 — Each thread tries to acquire the second lock and blocks, because the other thread holds it and will not release. Both threads are now BLOCKED forever. No CPU is used and no progress is made — the service hangs silently.

Step 4 — The DeadlockDetector, running every second, calls `ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads()`. It returns the two thread ids. The detector logs that a deadlock exists, naming each BLOCKED thread, the lock it waits for, and which thread holds that lock.

Step 5 — The demo then runs the SafeTransferService. Both safe threads compute the lock order from account id and always lock SAV2001 before CUR3001. Because both acquire locks in the same order, no cycle can form.

Step 6 — The safe transfers both complete and the demo logs success, proving consistent lock ordering eliminates the deadlock.

Final output:

```
2026-10-31 23:25:00 [INFO] txf-R-to-P locked SAV2001
2026-10-31 23:25:00 [INFO] txf-P-to-R locked CUR3001
2026-10-31 23:25:01 [SEVERE] DEADLOCK DETECTED among 2 threads:
2026-10-31 23:25:01 [SEVERE]   'txf-R-to-P' BLOCKED waiting for com.bank.jvm.Account@1b2 held by 'txf-P-to-R'
2026-10-31 23:25:01 [SEVERE]   'txf-P-to-R' BLOCKED waiting for com.bank.jvm.Account@9a1 held by 'txf-R-to-P'
2026-10-31 23:25:03 [WARNING] Naive transfers are deadlocked (see detector). Now the SAFE version:
2026-10-31 23:25:03 [INFO] safe-A-to-B completed SAV2001->CUR3001

2026-10-31 23:25:03 [INFO] SAFE transfers both completed with no deadlock
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  NAIVE (deadlock):
  txf-R-to-P: lock SAV2001 ──wait──▶ CUR3001 (held by other)
                  ▲                       │
                  │ circular wait         │
                  │                       ▼
  txf-P-to-R: lock CUR3001 ──wait──▶ SAV2001 (held by other)
         → both BLOCKED forever → service hangs
         → ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads() reports the cycle

  SAFE (ordered locking):
  both threads: lock lower id (SAV2001) FIRST, then CUR3001
  safe-A-to-B: lock SAV2001 → lock CUR3001 → transfer → release
  safe-B-to-A: wait for SAV2001 → lock SAV2001 → lock CUR3001 → transfer
         → no cycle possible → both complete
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Lock Ordering Design ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns / Principles ───────────────────────┐
  │  Resource ordering: global order on lock identity     │
  │     WHY: breaks circular-wait condition                │
  │  Alternative: tryLock(timeout) breaks hold-and-wait    │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Applied ──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: detector detects, service transfers               │
  │  O: swap NaiveTransferService → SafeTransferService    │
  │     without changing callers (same transfer() method)  │
  │  L: Safe/Naive interchangeable behind a transfer API   │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────┐ locks (ordered) ┌──────────────┐
  │ SafeTransferService  │────────────────▶│   Account    │
  │ + transfer(f,t,amt)  │  lower id first  │ + debit()    │
  │  first=min(ids)      │                  │ + credit()   │
  │  second=max(ids)     │                  └──────────────┘
  └──────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────┐ reads ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │   DeadlockDetector   │──────▶│ ThreadMXBean               │
  │ + checkOnce()        │       │ findDeadlockedThreads()    │
  │ + start()/stop()     │       │ getThreadInfo(ids,..)      │
  └──────────────────────┘       └──────────────────────────┘

  Call Chain (naive → detected → safe):
  1. t1 lock SAV2001; t2 lock CUR3001        [each holds one]
  2. t1 wait CUR3001; t2 wait SAV2001         [circular wait]
  3. detector.checkOnce() → DEADLOCK reported
  4. SafeTransferService: order by id → lock SAV2001 then CUR3001
  5. both safe transfers complete            [no cycle]
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A deadlock happens when two or more threads each hold a lock that another needs and none of them will release, so they all wait forever and make no progress. It needs four conditions at once — mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and a circular wait — and breaking any single one makes deadlock impossible. The most practical one to break is the circular wait. To diagnose a deadlock I take a thread dump with jstack or by sending the process a quit signal, and the deadlocked threads show up in the BLOCKED state, each one "waiting to lock" a monitor that another thread "holds." The HotSpot JVM is helpful here because it prints an explicit "Found one Java-level deadlock" section that names the threads and the locks, so I usually do not even have to trace the cycle by hand.

The fixes all come from breaking that circular wait. The cleanest is consistent lock ordering: I define a stable global order for locks, for example by account number, and always acquire them in that order so a cycle can never form. I also keep critical sections as short as possible and never call out to unknown code while holding a lock. When ordering is impractical, I use a ReentrantLock with tryLock and a timeout, so a thread that cannot get the second lock in time backs off, releases what it holds, and retries, which breaks the hold-and-wait condition. And for safety I add a runtime check using ThreadMXBean's findDeadlockedThreads, so if a deadlock ever forms in production it is detected, logged, and alerted instead of silently hanging.

In my banking work at National Bank of India, this was a real incident. Our transfer service hung with no errors and no CPU usage whenever two transfers ran at the same time in opposite directions, like Rajesh to Priya and Priya to Rajesh, because each thread locked its source account first and then blocked on the destination. The thread dump showed both threads BLOCKED in exactly that cycle. We fixed it by always locking the account with the lower account id first, which guarantees both transfers acquire the locks in the same order and the cycle can never happen. I also added the deadlock detector as a health check so we would catch any future ordering mistake immediately rather than discovering it from a frozen service.
